problem: "witnessed the outrages offered to its flag" softened to "watched ... insult its flag"; 'outrages' is the stronger word and should be kept.
replacement: The thirteen colonies that threw off the English yoke at the same moment, toward the end of the last century, had, as I have already observed, the same religion, the same language, the same customs, and almost the same laws. They were fighting a common enemy. These reasons were strong enough to unite them with one another and to consolidate them into one nation. But each colony had enjoyed a separate existence and a government under its own control, and the particular interests and customs that this system produced stood against a close and intimate union, which would have absorbed the individual importance of each into the general importance of all. Hence two opposite tendencies arose: one urged the Anglo-Americans to unite, the other to divide their strength. As long as the war with the mother country lasted, necessity kept the principle of union alive. The laws that established it were defective, yet the common tie held in spite of their flaws. *a But as soon as peace was concluded, the faults of the legislation became obvious, and the State seemed to dissolve all at once. Each colony became an independent republic and claimed absolute sovereignty. The Federal government had been condemned to impotence by its constitution, and a common danger no longer supported it. It witnessed the outrages offered to its flag by the great nations of Europe, and it could scarcely hold its ground against the Native American tribes or pay the interest on the debt contracted during the war of independence. It was already on the verge of collapse when it officially declared that it could not govern and appealed to the constituent authority of the nation. *b If America ever came near (however briefly) to that lofty pinnacle of glory to which its inhabitants like to point in their imagination, it was at the solemn moment when the power of the nation, so to speak, gave up its rule over the land. Every age has offered the spectacle of a people struggling vigorously to win its independence, and the efforts of the Americans in throwing off the English yoke have been greatly exaggerated. They were separated from their enemies by three thousand miles of ocean and backed by a powerful ally. The success of the United States may more fairly be credited to their geographical position than to the valor of their armies or the patriotism of their citizens. It would be ridiculous to compare the American war with the wars of the French Revolution, or the efforts of the Americans with those of the French. The French were attacked by the whole of Europe, without credit and without allies, and yet they were able to set a twentieth part of their population against the world, and to carry the torch of revolution beyond their frontiers while they smothered its devouring flame at home. But it is a novelty in the history of society to see a great people turn a calm and searching eye on itself when the legislature informs it that the wheels of government have stopped. It examines the extent of the evil with care and waits patiently for two whole years until a remedy is found, and it then adopts that remedy of its own free will, without having wrung a tear or a drop of blood from mankind. When the inadequacy of the first constitution was discovered, America had a double advantage: the calm that had followed the excitement of the revolution, and the great men who had led the revolution to a successful end. The assembly that took on the task of composing the second constitution was small, *c but George Washington was its President, and it held the finest talents and the noblest hearts the New World had ever produced. After long and careful deliberation, this national commission offered the people the body of general laws that still governs the Union. All the States adopted it one after another. *d The new Federal government began its functions in 1789, after an interregnum of two years. The American Revolution ended when the French Revolution began.

problem: First sentence left in 1862 wording ("which each State is to furnish", "fixed on").
replacement: n [ Every ten years Congress fixes anew the number of representatives each State is to send. The total number was 69 in 1789, and 240 in 1833. (See “American Almanac,” 1834, p. 194.) The Constitution decided that there should not be more than one representative for every 30,000 persons, but it set no minimum. Congress has not thought fit to increase the number of representatives in proportion to the growth of population. The first Act passed on the subject (April 14, 1792: see “Laws of the United States,” by Story, vol. i. p. 235) decided that there should be one representative for every 33,000 inhabitants. The last Act, passed in 1832, fixes the proportion at one for 48,000. The population represented is made up of all the free men and of three-fifths of the slaves.
